hint: This product has three kinds of pieces: plain numbers, powers of $x$ and powers of $y$. Treat each kind on its own.

hints.text: This product has three kinds of pieces: plain numbers, powers of $x$ and powers of $y$. Treat each kind on its own.

hints.title: 🪜 Try a simpler one
hints.text: Try one variable first: $(2x^3)(5x^4) = 10x^7$ — coefficients multiply, exponents add. Two variables just means running that same rule twice, once per letter.
Multiply the coefficients $3$ and $4$. Add the exponents of $x$, which are $2$ and $5$. Add the exponents of $y$, which are $3$ and $1$.
The pieces are $12$, $x^7$ and $y^4$, so the product is $12x^7y^4$, which is choice A.

explanation: Multiply the coefficients first, since the order of multiplication does not matter: $3 \times 4 = 12$.
Powers of the same base multiply by adding exponents, so $x^2 \cdot x^5 = x^7$.
A plain $y$ has exponent $1$, so adding the exponents of $y$ gives $y^3 \cdot y = y^4$.
Putting the three pieces together gives $12x^7y^4$, which is choice A.

alternativeExplanations.title: The invisible exponent
steps: Choice D is the trap: it forgets that the lone $y$ carries an exponent of $1$.
Any variable written without an exponent has an exponent of $1$, and any expression without a coefficient has a coefficient of $1$.
Writing those in explicitly before you start costs a second and prevents the most common slip in this question type.

alternativeExplanations.title: ⚠️ The trap here
steps: Choice D forgets that the bare y carries an invisible exponent 1, so y³·y should become y⁴.
Rewrite y as y¹ before adding exponents. Making the invisible exponent visible costs one second and removes the trap entirely.
